chunks: "My rules of thumb start from the fact that copper is just a resistor.
One ounce copper is about half a milliohm per square, so I think in squares: a trace that is 50 squares long is 25 milliohms, and at 10 amps that is a quarter of a volt and 2.
5 watts. That's already a lot, so rule one is short and wide, and wherever I can I use a pour or a plane instead of a trace. Rule two is size it properly.

I pick a temperature rise, say 10 to 20 degrees, and use the IPC-2221 or IPC-2152 charts for the width, then I separately check the voltage drop against what the load can tolerate, because that often needs more copper than the heating limit does.
Outer layers carry more current per width than inner layers since they cool better.

Rule three is watch the weak links: use several vias in parallel when current changes layers, not one; don't neck the trace down at pads; use direct connections or wide spokes on power pads instead of tiny thermal reliefs; and make sure the connector has enough pins.
Last, route the return with the same care, keep the loop small, and keep noisy high-current paths away from sensitive analog.
If it's really big I'll go to 2 oz copper, add solder or a bus bar, and check it with a thermal camera on the first board."
